pr_title: Bluetooth: fix HCI command / data deadlock
pr_body:
See commits for more info. 
TLDR: makes the ACL fragmentation asynchronous, freeing the TX thread for sending commands when the ACL buffers are full.

Fixes #25917
pr_comments: @runegrunnet could you please take a look?

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/37577 was very useful for reproducing the deadlock in simulation, so thanks a lot @prathje ! You might want to review this as well, or try it on hardware.

> #37577 was very useful for reproducing the deadlock in simulation, so thanks a lot @prathje ! You might want to review this as well, or try it on hardware.

comments:
Anylsis:
Symmetrical deadlock in both devices in the connection between TX and RX thread.
TX thread has filled up the all the buffers in the controller and has blocked waiting for num complete events.
Controller has filled up all it's receive buffers and the RX thread is delivering ACL packets as fast as it can. 
The RX thread receives an HCI event (phy update complete) and blocks on sending an HCI command waiting for the TX thread to send the command.
The TX thread will not be able to proceed until a num complete arrives on both sides.
The RX thread will not be able to proceed until TX thread is unblocked on both sides.
Receive buffer is full on both sides so no new packets can be transmitted, meaning no new completes will happen.
I ran into this issue and my workaround was to do the sending from a workqueue thread with a lower priority.
@xudongzheng Could you elaborate on your workaround? What exactly did you move to the workqueue? Sending of data, or sending of the command?

@xudongzheng That behavior is documented here: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/include/bluetooth/gatt.h#L927L930

That is however not the same as is happening in this case, you haven't encountered this issue.

I'm seeing the same thing when I spam bt_gatt_notify.  This seems like a dangerous bug since there's no way to really know if you'll exceed the threshold for overflow.  Much better would be to simply return an error that could optionally be ignored for non-critical notifications. @galak can you comment on why you feel this is low priority?

> The RX thread receives an HCI event (phy update complete) and blocks on sending an HCI command waiting for the TX thread to send the command.

I can't understand this, can you point out the relevant code?
@joerchan Why we `hci_le_read_max_data_len`  not use `bt_hci_cmd_send` to avoiding race condition ?

> I'm seeing the same thing when I spam bt_gatt_notify. This seems like a dangerous bug since there's no way to really know if you'll exceed the threshold for overflow. Much better would be to simply return an error that could optionally be ignored for non-critical notifications. @galak can you comment on why you feel this is low priority?

I also see this. Whenever I see `Unable to allocate TX context` the nRF52 I I control over HCI completely freezes. My bt_gatt_notify is now in a workqueue but if I decrease the notification speed to anything below 500ms the system still deadlocks.   It's totally bizarre.
@cvinayak and I could generate the same assertion error using the sample in #37577

So I think I could isolate causes of the mentioned assertion fail (at least in my case).
First, I am running BabbleSim and probably need to enable flow control manually:
```
CONFIG_BT_HCI_ACL_FLOW_CONTROL=y
```

Second (and more important), I was sending whole SDU segments over an L2CAP channel which I assumed would not be fragmented as I was using the channel's MTU as the maximum payload size. As it turns out, the packets did in fact not fit into the ACL buffers and were thus also getting fragmented again. With a restricted amount of buffers available for fragmentation (see https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/reference/kconfig/CONFIG_BT_L2CAP_TX_FRAG_COUNT.html) this seems to have favored the sem_take timeout.

I am currently using the following config:
```
CONFIG_BT_L2CAP_TX_MTU=247
CONFIG_BT_BUF_ACL_RX_SIZE=256
CONFIG_BT_BUF_ACL_TX_SIZE=251
CONFIG_BT_HCI_ACL_FLOW_CONTROL=y
```

And changed my mtu calculation to actually incorporate the BT_L2CAP_SDU_TX_MTU:
```c
uint32_t mtu = MIN(le_chan.tx.mtu, BT_L2CAP_SDU_TX_MTU);
```

Another reason might be mentioned in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/34600: if many transmissions are scheduled rapidly, the number of TX buffers could get exhausted (have not yet confirmed this).
```
CONFIG_BT_L2CAP_TX_BUF_COUNT=128
```

@klapro this is supposed to be fixed. Could you open a new bug report with all the relevant details (how to reproduce etc) ? Maybe it's something different.

review_comments:
It is actually slightly confusing that we use `frag` here as `struct net_buf *`, but also have a boolean `bool frag` in `struct tx_meta` - Especially when we are doing the NULL check like this (would be more obvious if this was `if (frag != NULL)`. 

Otherwise could consider renaming the `bool frag` to `bool is_frag`
yes. I will probably rename it.
The type of the variable being assigned to (`tx_data[i]`) is already uint8_t, so truncation happens either way, ie the explicit typecast is redundant.
at least with the cast it's visible that it's on purpose and not a mistake
Maybe add a code comment above this, something along the lines of "Since we used peek(), the queue still owns the reference to the buffer, so we need to take an explicit additional reference here.

> At the very least, in addition to asserting that buf != NULL, you should also `BT_ASSERT((buf->flags & NET_BUF_FRAGS) == 0);`. Though even that's pretty unclean, since these are really net_buf-internal features.

Oh, and in addition to the assert, you need to explicitly set `buf->frags = NULL` since the k_fifo implementation leaves the linked list pointer untouched when removing from the list.

Also see https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/38830#pullrequestreview-763305021 and related discussion in the PR.
is that really a problem since I'm using the `_get` before passing it to `bt_send`? That takes care of the fragments, and the peek is a non-destructive operation afaik.

At the very least you need to clear the `buf->frags` pointer since `k_fifo_peek_head()` doesn't do that for you. You have the `EIO` branch below where e.g. `net_buf_unref()` is called, and `net_buf_unref()` will also unref the frags pointer if it is non-NULL. Same goes for any other net_buf API calls you might do on the buffer before calling `net_buf_get()`

Actually, I just realised that the `EIO` branch is probably buggy in this regard, i.e. if `send_buf()` returns error before getting to the `net_buf_get()` phase, you have a pointer to something that's still in the FIFO and you don't own a reference to, yet you still call `net_buf_unref()` on it.

This `frags` business is really backwards IMO, why do we even use it? seems like a linked-list implementation that we then put on another linked-list (the queue)?
Then we need all those safe APIs to deal with that instead of being able to just use the fifo/queue apis directly.
anyway for the EIO case, the buffer has already been consumed by the `_get`.
Why do we want to clear the `frags` ptr again? isn't anything in `frags` actually part of the current buffer?

> Why do we want to clear the frags ptr again? isn't anything in frags actually part of the current buffer?

Yes, but only if those buffers were removed from the FIFO that they were passed through. If you use k_fifo APIs directly you may end up with a frags pointing at buffers that are still inside the FIFO, i.e. it's the FIFO that owns their references, not the parent buffer. Since we don't use frags (it's a feature added by the networking stack folks) we could for now just assert that frags were not used and then explicitly set the buf->frags pointer to NULL.

Anyway, as I said, really the cleanest way out of this would be to detach the frags from being in a union together with the linked list pointer in net_buf. But that's also considerably more work, more intrusive (affecting things outside of Bluetooth) and also comes with an increased memory footprint.

> This frags business is really backwards IMO, why do we even use it? seems like a linked-list implementation that we then put on another linked-list (the queue)?

You'll have to ask the networking subsystem folks about that. I don't think they use FIFOs as much as we do, but then they do have an abstraction called net_pkt which has a pointer to the "top" buffer, which may then have a fragment list.

> anyway for the EIO case, the buffer has already been consumed by the _get.

Even then, this code looks pretty fragile, and could break if it's modified by someone not intimately familiar with net_buf internals. Anyway, if you make sure you always own a reference to the buffer when having a pointer to it (i.e. call net_buf_ref() after peek()) then the code becomes more future-proof.

I also thought we weren't using frags (ie I had an assert doing just that before), but there seem to be some use of it in `l2cap.c` regarding SDU handling.
I'm not sure I'm reading the code correctly though, so I'd appreciate if you took a look just to double-check.

One compromise I just thought of: maybe we could introduce a new CONFIG_NET_BUF_FRAGS option to enable/disable net_buf fragments support. Since we don't use/need it, we could keep it disabled, as long as you don't enable some other subsystem that depends on it (like the networking stack itself).

> introduce a new CONFIG_NET_BUF_FRAGS option 

Well, that'd take care of the memory overhead that'd come with `frags` being outside of the union, but we'd still need to use the proper APIs so that our code doesn't break if the option is enabled.

> Even then, this code looks pretty fragile, and could break if it's modified by someone not intimately familiar with net_buf internals.

I think this can be argued for the whole BT host. I know I've broken a bunch of stuff because of hidden assumptions like these.
I thought about moving the error handling somewhere else, but all the other places seemed messy as well. I'll at least add the referencing (and frags assert) as you said.

> I also thought we weren't using frags (ie I had an assert doing just that before), but there seem to be some use of it in l2cap.c regarding SDU handling.

Right, I had forgotten about that. IIRC that's code for 6LoWPAN/IPSP when we receive buffers from the Networking subsystem that we should then send over L2CAP Connection-oriented Channels. In such a case the Net subsystem might feed us with fragment lists.
It looks like the `l2cap.c` frags code stays within the L2CAP layer, i.e. when passing to ACL (conn->tx_queue) there are no fragment buffers anymore.

thanks for looking into it. that was my initial understanding as well, just wanted to be sure, since we pass the buffers around and I'm not always sure what we do with those frags.

I will add the assert when we put the buffers in the queue, I think it's safer.

I think it's better to have the assert close to the code that's relying on the condition that you're asserting. Otherwise the code will end up looking like it's potentially broken, and to figure out it's not you have to understand to look at another place (the writing side of the FIFO).
Can I have it at both places? because good luck getting a stack trace of who put that bad buffer in if that assert hits when popping it rather than when pushing it in.
Yes, that's fine. We could make the writing side a runtime check too, if we consider this the public API for that layer.

> Oh, and in addition to the assert, you need to explicitly set buf->frags = NULL since the k_fifo implementation leaves the linked list pointer untouched when removing from the list.

I just tried and it didn't work. I think it's because `buf->frags` is in a union with the node ptr. 
So if I overwrite it with `NULL` while it is still on the queue, and it ends up that I don't pull it from the fifo (e.g. the sem_take fails), the fifo list is effectively broken.
Right, good point. And this is another reason why using peak() together with the union is bad - you end up with the buffer in an inconsistent state until you actually remove it from from the FIFO.
The short term solution would then probably be to document this clearly and try to make the code flow path from peek() to get() as short and obvious as possible.
yep agreed. I will place a comment above the `peek` saying this.
so I reverted the assert since #52760 got merged.
